title: HE WENT DOWN INTO THE PIT — The Lion, the Snow, and the Kind of Faith That Refuses to Run
paragraphs: HE WENT DOWN INTO THE PIT — The Lion, the Snow, and the Kind of Faith That Refuses to Run

Benaiah stepped into a place most men would have desperately tried to escape. But the greatest truth buried in this strange, violent, unforgettable moment is not that Christians should become fearless lion-killers. It is that sometimes faithfulness to God means going down when every instinct in you is screaming to run—and discovering that the pit does not get the final word.
There is one sentence in the Bible that sounds almost too cinematic to be real.
A lion.
A pit.
Snow falling.
And a man going down.
Not climbing out.
Going down.
Read that again, because something about those words should bother you.
Most of us spend our lives trying to get out of pits.
Benaiah went into one.
Second Samuel 23:20 records:

“And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel, who had done many acts, he slew two lionlike men of Moab: he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow.”
The Hebrew preserves the starkness of the moment:
וְהוּא יָרַד וְהִכָּה אֶת־הָאֲרִי בְּתוֹךְ הַבֹּאר בְּיוֹם הַשָּׁלֶג
Vehu yarad vehikkah et-ha’ari betokh habbor beyom hashaleg.
In straightforward English:
“And he went down and struck the lion in the midst of the pit on a day of snow.”
There is no long speech.
No explanation of what Benaiah was feeling.
No promise recorded beforehand that he would survive.

Scripture does not tell us that he chased the lion. It does not tell us exactly why he entered the pit. It does not give us the dimensions of the pit, the depth of the snow, or the thoughts racing through his mind.
And we should resist the temptation to make the Bible say what it does not say.
What it does say is already astonishing enough.
He went down.
The Hebrew verb is יָרַד — yārad.
To descend.
To go down.
And suddenly this ancient warrior begins to feel uncomfortably close to home.
Because maybe you know something about going down.
Maybe your lion did not have claws.
Maybe it came through a telephone call.
A betrayal.
A diagnosis.
A funeral.
A marriage quietly collapsing behind smiling photographs.
A child walking away from God.
An addiction you promised Jesus you would never touch again.
A secret browser history.
A private compromise.
A debt nobody knows about.
A ministry wound.
A prayer that seems to have disappeared into the ceiling.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong because you have become very good at bleeding where nobody can see it.
You still go to church.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still share the verse.
Still smile.
Still answer, “I’m fine.”
But somewhere beneath the public version of you there is a pit.
And something is roaring inside it.
That is why Benaiah's story is dangerous when misunderstood.
It would be easy to turn it into another motivational slogan:
“Chase your lions!”
“Conquer your fears!”
“Become unstoppable!”
But the Gospel is not Christianity-flavored self-help.
Jesus did not die and rise again merely to turn insecure people into confident people.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
The deepest lion stalking humanity is not low self-esteem, missed opportunity, or lack of courage.
Our deepest problem is sin.
And no amount of human bravery can kill it.
That changes how we read Benaiah.

Benaiah's courage is real and worthy of remembrance. Second Samuel places him among David's mighty warriors and records that his exploits brought him honor. David eventually placed him over his guard.
But Benaiah is not Jesus.
And that distinction matters.
Because eventually even the bravest warrior needs a Savior.
You can conquer enemies and still be unable to cleanse your own heart.
You can build a career and still be enslaved in secret.
You can win arguments and lose your soul.
You can become respected by everybody around you while hiding from the God who already sees everything.
You can even become religious enough to disguise rebellion as righteousness.
That is the scandal beneath all our carefully managed appearances:
We cannot save ourselves.
And then comes grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that winks at sin.
Not grace that tells us to remain exactly as we are.
Grace with scars in its hands.
Grace that calls sinners to repentance.
Grace that forgives the guilty because Another bore their judgment.
Grace that finds Peter after his denial.
Grace that meets Saul while he is persecuting Christians.
Grace that welcomes the prodigal home.
Grace that says to people covered in shame, “Come.”
This is where the story of the pit begins pointing beyond Benaiah.
Because centuries later, the Son of David would come.
Not merely one of David's mighty men.
David's Lord.
Jesus Christ.
And His victory would dwarf every battlefield achievement recorded in Israel's history.
Christ did not descend into our world because we were impressive enough to deserve Him.
He came for sinners.
He entered our suffering.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Buried.
And when humanity's greatest enemy appeared to have swallowed Him whole, the grave discovered something no lion, army, empire, demon, or tomb could change:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
He rose.
That is the center of Christianity.
Not “believe in yourself.”
Believe in Christ.
Not “discover the warrior within.”
Die to yourself and follow the King.
Not “you are strong enough.”
His grace is sufficient.
Benaiah entered a pit containing a lion and emerged alive.
Jesus entered death itself and rose victorious—and everyone united to Him by faith receives what no human warrior could ever earn: forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs more than another motivational speech.
You are exhausted from trying to be your own Benaiah.
You have fought the same temptation so many times that you are embarrassed to confess it again.
You have promised God things at midnight and broken those promises before breakfast.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to lift your hands.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
But when everything becomes quiet, you know exactly where the lion lives.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend the lion is a kitten.
It tells you where to run when you finally admit you cannot save yourself.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the lie that hiding can heal you.
Confession is not informing an ignorant God.
He already knows.
It is stepping into the light before the One who knows the worst thing about you and still commands you to come through Christ.
Maybe your courageous step today is not something dramatic.
Maybe it is finally saying:
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
Maybe it is confessing what you keep renaming.
Maybe it is deleting what keeps feeding your temptation.
Maybe it is asking another mature believer for help.
Maybe it is forgiving someone while still maintaining wise boundaries.
Maybe it is returning to Scripture after months of spiritual numbness.
Maybe it is praying again after disappointment made prayer feel dangerous.
Maybe courage is simply obeying God while your hands are still shaking.
Because biblical courage is not the absence of fear.
And faith is not confidence that every earthly story will end the way you want.
Sometimes God delivers His people from danger.
Sometimes He sustains them through it.
Hebrews 11 celebrates people who experienced extraordinary deliverance—and in the same chapter honors faithful believers who suffered terribly without receiving earthly rescue.
So we cannot turn Benaiah's lion into a formula:
“Be brave enough and God will make everything work out.”
Scripture promises something better than that.
God Himself.
Christ Himself.
Grace sufficient for the valley.
A resurrection beyond the grave.
A Kingdom that suffering cannot cancel.
This means your snowy day does not prove that God abandoned you.
Your pit does not automatically mean you missed His will.
Your tears do not make you faithless.
Your weakness does not surprise Him.
And the fact that you need help does not disqualify you from grace.
But there is another side to this story that comfortable Christianity would rather avoid.
Sometimes obedience requires movement.
וְהוּא יָרַד — vehu yarad.
“And he went down.”
There are moments when endlessly discussing obedience becomes another form of disobedience.
You already know what Scripture says.
Forgive.
Confess.
Flee sexual immorality.
Love your enemy.
Care for the vulnerable.
Speak truth.
Stop lying.
Put away bitterness.
Return what is not yours.
Turn from pornography.
Stop feeding the secret relationship.
Stop worshiping money.
Stop making an idol out of people's approval.
Pray.
Serve.
Give.
Follow Christ.
And sometimes we remain standing at the edge asking God for another confirmation because obedience below looks frightening.
Perhaps the issue is no longer that God's Word is unclear.
Perhaps you are afraid of what obedience will cost.
That is a different problem.
Jesus never marketed discipleship as painless.
He said, “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
A cross is not an accessory.
It is an instrument of death.
Following Jesus means the old ruler of your life has to lose his throne.
You.
Your appetites.
Your pride.
Your reputation.
Your demand to control the outcome.
Your insistence that God explain everything before you obey anything.
And this is where grace becomes far more beautiful than religious performance.
God does not tell sinners to clean themselves perfectly and then approach Christ.
We come because we cannot clean ourselves.
We repent because His kindness leads us there.
We obey not to purchase salvation, but because salvation has changed our allegiance.
The Christian does not fight for acceptance with God as though enough victories could finally make the Father love us.
Those who are in Christ fight from grace.
That distinction can save someone from years of spiritual exhaustion.
You are not climbing toward a cross trying to persuade Jesus to love you.
The cross is the announcement of how far divine love went to rescue sinners.
And resurrection is the announcement that sin and death do not have the final word.
From scandal...
to grace.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never mattered.
He rewrites your future by paying for sin with His own blood and raising you into newness of life.
Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
Neither was Paul's.
Neither was the thief's.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, neither does yours have to be.
But do not confuse grace with permission to stay chained.
The Jesus who forgives also says, “Follow Me.”
Grace has feet.
Grace gets up.
Grace leaves the old life behind.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace turns confession into transformation.
Grace makes former slaves into sons and daughters who learn, sometimes painfully and gradually, how to walk in freedom.
Maybe you are reading this while fighting something nobody knows about.
Then stop performing for one moment.
No Christian mask.
No polished testimony.
No pretending.
What is roaring in your pit?
Pornography?
Bitterness?
Adultery?
Envy?
Alcohol?
Pride?
Fear?
Unforgiveness?
Greed?
Secret unbelief?
The desperate need to be admired?
Or maybe it is not a sinful habit at all.
Maybe your pit is grief.
Loneliness.
Rejection.
Exhaustion.
The ache of waiting.
A prayer that has gone unanswered so long that hope itself now hurts.
Bring that too.
Jesus is not frightened by your honesty.
The Psalms prove that God's people can cry, question, lament, and still cling to Him.
You do not have to manufacture strength for Christ.
You need Christ.
And perhaps the most courageous prayer you can pray tonight contains only five words:
“Jesus, I need You again.”
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, do not write an impressive comment.
Write an honest one.
Or tell your testimony. Someone scrolling beneath this article may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores broken people.
And please understand why sharing matters.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Christ purchased redemption—not us.
But if biblical truth has helped you, sharing it can place that truth before someone you could never reach with a sermon.
Send it privately to the believer who stopped attending church.
Send it to the person who thinks his scandal has made grace impossible.
Support Gospel Warrior because you want more people confronted with Scripture and pointed toward Jesus—not because supporting a ministry somehow earns merit before God.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a page.
Not merchandise.
Jesus.
If supporting Gospel-centered work is one way you choose to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, then support it generously. But never mistake the messenger for the Savior.
The goal is not to build people who cannot live without Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward Christ until they understand that without Him, they have nothing.
And perhaps that brings us back to the snow.
Imagine the scene one final time.
Cold air.
White ground.
A dark opening.
A lion somewhere below.
And a man standing above it.
Scripture does not tell us how long Benaiah stood there.
It only tells us what he eventually did.
יָרַד.
Yārad.
He went down.
Years later, people remembered his name.
But thousands of years later, his story can remind us of something greater than human courage.
Your life will contain pits you never selected.
Some lions should be fled because Scripture commands us to flee temptation.
Some dangers require wisdom rather than confrontation.
Some battles require pastors, doctors, counselors, authorities, friends, or professional help.
Biblical faith is not recklessness.
But when obedience to God clearly requires you to move...
move.
When repentance requires confession...
confess.
When forgiveness requires surrendering vengeance...
release it to God.
When faithfulness requires standing alone...
stand.
When following Jesus costs you the approval you worshiped...
follow Jesus anyway.
Not because you are Benaiah.
Because Christ is Lord.
And when you fail—and sometimes you will—do not build your home inside the pit.
Repent.
Get up.
Come back to Jesus.
There is blood enough at the cross for repentant sinners.
There is power enough in the risen Christ for another beginning.
There is grace enough for the person who thought the scandal had become the final chapter.
It hasn't.
The lion is memorable.
The pit is unforgettable.
The snow makes the scene cinematic.
But the deepest truth is greater than all three:
The place that looks like the end of your story may become the place where you discover that Jesus was never finished writing it.
Because after the roaring stops, after the snow melts, after the applause disappears and every human warrior eventually lays down his strength, only one victory remains eternally undefeated:
The empty tomb still says your darkest chapter does not get to write the ending when Jesus Christ holds the pen.
